inputs.need:
I work as a health services researcher in our hospital's patient flow command centre, which opened in March 2025. Every admitted emergency department patient gets a boarding-risk score when the admission decision is entered, and patients above the threshold are flagged on the command centre's wall display so that the bed managers can escalate them. The vendor says the score identifies patients who will board for more than four hours, but nobody here has checked. Median boarding time is still 5.1 hours, and the emergency physicians think the flag mostly marks patients everyone already knew would wait, while quieter medical patients near the threshold get missed.

I want to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the flag against what actually happened: the reference standard would be boarding of four hours or more, measured from the admission decision to departure from the emergency department using the timestamps. I need its sensitivity and specificity at the threshold the command centre uses, whether the score is calibrated for our patients, and whether accuracy differs at night, at weekends, and between medical and surgical admissions. I also want to know what published work exists on predicting boarding or inpatient bed waits, because the vendor's documentation cites only its own validation. We cannot change the score itself, and the command centre's data analyst can give us one day a week.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; the score cannot be changed or retrained during the evaluation; the command centre analyst is available one day a week until June 2027; data come only from existing timestamps and the score log.
localFacts: The command centre has logged every boarding-risk score and flag since March 2025, about 21,000 admission decisions a year.
Median boarding time from admission decision to emergency department departure was 5.1 hours in the last quarter.
The data governance office approved use of command centre logs and emergency timestamps for service evaluation on 2026-08-28 (approval DG-2026-311).
The command centre analyst is available one day a week until June 2027.

records.title: Predicting prolonged emergency department boarding at the time of the admission decision: development and external validation of a logistic model
records.authors: Osei-Whitfield R, Brandt-Nakamura E, Delgado-Hughes P
records.abstract: We developed a logistic model predicting boarding of more than four hours from nine predictors available at the admission decision, including hour, weekday, admitting service and inpatient occupancy, using 48,200 admissions at one hospital, and validated it at a second hospital. Discrimination fell from a c statistic of 0.78 in development to 0.71 in validation. Calibration was poor in the validation hospital, where 58 percent of patients boarded more than four hours against a mean predicted risk of 44 percent. Recalibration of the intercept corrected most of the difference. The authors advise local recalibration before any model is used.

records.title: External validation of a commercial boarding prediction tool in three hospitals
records.authors: Kowalewski-Adeyemi T, Lindgren-Soto M, Haddad-Pereira N
records.abstract: We validated a commercial boarding prediction tool in 61,400 admission decisions at three hospitals that did not contribute to its development. At the vendor's recommended threshold, sensitivity for boarding of four hours or more was 0.62 (95 percent CI 0.60 to 0.64) and specificity 0.71 (95 percent CI 0.70 to 0.72). Sensitivity was 0.49 for admission decisions made at night and 0.66 during the day. Calibration differed between hospitals and was worst in the busiest one. The tool's own published validation had used only its development sites.

records.title: A hospital command centre and emergency department boarding: an interrupted time series
records.abstract: A 600-bed hospital opened a patient flow command centre with a live display of flagged admitted patients. In an interrupted time series over 36 months, mean boarding hours per admitted patient fell from 6.2 to 5.4 after the opening, with no change in the pre-existing trend. The study did not assess the accuracy of the flags that directed the command centre's work, and a new discharge lounge opened three months later. The authors could not say which parts of the command centre produced the change.

records.title: Occupancy, not patient characteristics, drives emergency department boarding time: a multilevel analysis
records.abstract: In 27,900 admissions over two years, inpatient occupancy at the hour of the admission decision explained most of the variation in boarding time between days. Adding patient characteristics to a model with occupancy and time of day raised the c statistic only from 0.74 to 0.76. Boarding over four hours occurred on 81 percent of days when occupancy exceeded 92 percent. The authors suggest that tools flagging individual patients mostly identify busy days rather than patients who need escalation, and that occupancy should be the comparison for any patient-level score.

records.title: Spectrum effects in predicting hospital bed waits: accuracy by admitting service and time of day
records.abstract: We examined the accuracy of a bed wait prediction score across patient groups in 19,300 admission decisions. At a fixed threshold, sensitivity for waits of four hours or more was 0.68 for medical admissions and 0.51 for surgical admissions, and specificity was higher for surgical admissions. Accuracy was lowest for admissions decided between midnight and 06:00. Reporting a single overall sensitivity hid these differences. The authors recommend reporting accuracy separately by admitting service and time of day in any evaluation of such scores.

records.title: Reference standards for boarding time: agreement between emergency department timestamps and bed management records
records.abstract: We compared emergency department departure timestamps with bed management records and direct observation for 2,400 admitted patients. The departure timestamp was recorded on average 22 minutes after the patient physically left, and 7 percent of admissions had no departure time. Near the four-hour threshold, these delays misclassified about 5 percent of patients as prolonged boarders. Using the bed management arrival time on the ward as a check reduced misclassification. The authors recommend a documented reference standard with a rule for missing times.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records from the second search, appraised at abstract level; the first search reported two hits but returned no records, and four model leads remain unchecked. External validation of a commercial boarding tool found moderate sensitivity and specificity at the vendor threshold, with much lower sensitivity at night; a developed model lost discrimination and calibration at an external hospital; sensitivity differed by admitting service; and occupancy, rather than patient characteristics, explained most boarding variation. Timestamps used as the reference standard are late and sometimes missing, which misclassifies patients near the four-hour threshold. A command centre was followed by fewer boarding hours in one hospital, but no study linked flag accuracy to that change. The records support a local accuracy study with a documented reference standard and results by time of day and service.
response.gradeRationale: Observational validation studies of different tools in other hospitals, with inconsistent calibration and indirectness to the local score; certainty that the local flag performs like the published tools is low.

response.reading: The flag sits between the admission decision and the bed managers' escalation. Its value depends on identifying the patients who will board and who can be helped, but occupancy explains most boarding, published tools lose accuracy at night and differ by admitting service, and the reference standard itself depends on late and missing timestamps. A local accuracy study must therefore define the reference standard carefully and report the flag's performance where escalation can act.

response.rationale: The question is how well a deployed index test (the flag) classifies a target condition (boarding of four hours or more) against a reference standard, which is a diagnostic accuracy design applied to a prognostic flag. External validation of a similar tool (c1), calibration loss at external sites (c2), reference standard error (c3) and spectrum effects (c4) shape the protocol.

response.overview: Diagnostic accuracy study of a deployed boarding-risk flag, using a consecutive series of all admission decisions from March 2025 to February 2027 with complete verification against a documented timestamp reference standard.
response.population: All adult admission decisions in the emergency department in the period (about 38,000); decisions later cancelled or transferred to another hospital are excluded and counted.
response.exposure: Index test: the flag at the deployed threshold, as logged at the admission decision; the underlying score is used for calibration and discrimination.
response.procedures: The analyst links the score log to emergency timestamps and ward arrival times. The reference standard is boarding of four hours or more from the admission decision to emergency department departure; when departure is missing or more than 60 minutes after ward arrival, ward arrival minus 10 minutes is used, and the rule is fixed before analysis. Escalation by bed managers is recorded from the command centre log. The analyst who applies the reference standard rule does not see the flag.

outcomes.name: Sensitivity and specificity of the flag at the deployed threshold
outcomes.measure: Proportions with 95 percent confidence intervals against the reference standard, reported as a pair
outcomes.why: The flag is used as a binary signal; both errors matter to escalation.

outcomes.name: Calibration of the score
outcomes.measure: Calibration intercept and slope, and a calibration plot by decile of predicted risk
outcomes.why: Miscalibration was common at external sites (claim c2).

outcomes.name: Discrimination compared with occupancy alone
outcomes.measure: c statistic of the score and of an occupancy and time-of-day model
outcomes.why: Tests whether the score adds to occupancy.

outcomes.name: Escalations triggered by false-positive flags
outcomes.measure: Number of escalations per week for patients who did not board four hours
outcomes.why: The workload cost of the flag's errors.

outcomes.name: Reference standard completeness
outcomes.measure: Proportion of decisions needing the missing-time rule
outcomes.why: Shows how much the reference standard depends on the rule (claim c3).

response.theoreticalFramework: None; STARD 2015 and TRIPOD structure the accuracy and validation reporting.
response.summary: Consecutive-series accuracy study with a fixed reference standard rule, calibration and spectrum reporting.

response.designSummary: Accuracy estimates against a timestamp reference standard, with calibration and discrimination analyses and subgroup estimates by time of day, weekday and admitting service.
response.sampleSize: About 38,000 admission decisions over two years, with more than half expected to board four hours or more given a median of 5.1 hours, give confidence intervals of about one percentage point for overall sensitivity and specificity. The binding constraint is the smallest subgroup: night-time surgical decisions, perhaps 2,000, still give intervals of about four percentage points. Because boarding clusters by day through occupancy, intervals use day-level cluster-robust standard errors, which widen them by an amount estimated from the data. More than 100 events in every subgroup meets the usual minimum for calibration assessment.
response.primaryAnalysis: Sensitivity and specificity of the flag at the deployed threshold with 95 percent confidence intervals using day-level cluster-robust standard errors; the pair is reported together with the number of true and false positives per 1,000 admission decisions.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Calibration intercept, slope and plot; c statistic of the score and of an occupancy and time-of-day model with the difference and its interval; accuracy by time of day, weekday and admitting service; sensitivity analysis excluding escalated patients.
response.missingData: Decisions with missing departure times use the pre-specified ward-arrival rule; decisions with neither time are excluded and counted, and a sensitivity analysis treats them first as boarded and then as not boarded.
response.multiplicity: One primary pair; subgroup estimates are reported with intervals and an interaction test, not as separate claims.
response.software: R with the pROC and sandwich packages.
overfittingGuards: Reference standard rule fixed before analysis
Threshold taken as deployed, not re-optimised
Subgroups limited to three pre-specified variables
No retraining or recalibration reported as the main result
response.summary: About 38,000 decisions give narrow intervals; the smallest subgroup and day-level clustering set the precision.

response.risks: No contact with patients; the risk is misuse of results, for example ranking bed managers or units, which is avoided by reporting at hospital level.
response.consent: Individual consent is not sought for this service evaluation of existing logs under the data governance approval; patients are informed through the hospital's notice on the use of operational data.
response.data: Linked data on the hospital analytics server, with record numbers replaced by study codes before analysis; no data leave the hospital.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients admitted at night, older patients and those admitted to services with lower sensitivity may be systematically missed by the flag. Accuracy is reported by time of day and admitting service, and by age group, so that the command centre can see whom the flag fails.
response.effectiveness: The evaluation is useful whether the flag performs well or badly; a poor result redirects escalation effort.
response.efficiency: Existing logs and about 25 analyst days.
response.grants: None needed for the evaluation; a later recalibration or new model could seek funding.
response.partnerships: Command centre staff, emergency and inpatient physicians, bed managers, and a patient partner from the hospital's patient and family advisory council.
response.rebPath: Service evaluation of operational data under data governance approval DG-2026-311; before publication the hospital research ethics board will be asked whether review is required, following the TCPS 2 guidance on program evaluation.
response.limitations: One hospital; escalation may bias accuracy downward; the reference standard depends on timestamps.
response.summary: Evaluation of existing logs under data governance approval, with equity reporting by time of day, service and age.

response.partnershipPlan: A patient partner who waited overnight in the emergency department and a bed manager review the reference standard definition and the plain-language summary.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; complaints about waits for a bed over the last year are themed by time of day.

response.title: Accuracy of a deployed boarding-risk flag in a hospital patient flow command centre: a diagnostic accuracy study
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the sensitivity, specificity and calibration of a vendor boarding-risk flag used by a patient flow command centre. Design: consecutive series of admission decisions from March 2025 to February 2027 with a documented timestamp reference standard (boarding of four hours or more). Results and conclusions will be written after the analysis.
response.introduction: Command centres flag patients at risk of prolonged boarding, but published validations of such tools show moderate accuracy that falls at night and varies by service, and the local tool has only vendor validation.
response.methods: Score log linked to emergency timestamps and ward arrival times; reference standard rule fixed in advance and applied blind to the flag; sensitivity and specificity at the deployed threshold with day-level cluster-robust intervals; calibration; comparison with occupancy alone; subgroups by time of day, weekday and service.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present the flow of admission decisions, the two-by-two table, accuracy by subgroup, calibration plots and the occupancy comparison.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret the flag's accuracy against published validations, weigh the treatment paradox from escalation, and state what the command centre should change.
response.limitations: One hospital; escalation bias; timestamp-based reference standard.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will be limited to the flag's accuracy and will not claim that the command centre reduced boarding.
response.reportingChecklist: TRIPOD, with STARD 2015 items for the binary flag
response.summary: TRIPOD-structured draft with results left empty until analysis.
